card.profile: Pulimaranja Thondachan, also known as Kari Kurikal, is a deity worshipped and performed as theyyam by the Pulayar community in the North Malabar region of Kerala, India. The tradition is rooted in the legend of Madai Kari Kurikkal, a man who possessed the magical skill to change his body into a leopard. After a tragic misunderstanding where he killed his frightened wife, he disappeared into the forest and became a revered spiritual figure. This powerful myth has also inspired modern regional culture, notably through the play and film Pulijanmam.
card.insight: In the folklore of North Malabar, the mortal Madai Kari Kurikkal famously mastered animal transformation in eighteen kalaris before vanishing into the forest.

card.profile_long:
Pulimaranja Thondachan, also known by the name Kari Kurikal, represents a sacred deity worshipped within the North Malabar region of Kerala, specifically spanning the present-day districts of Kannur and Kasargod. This tradition is practiced and performed as theyyam, holding deep religious significance for the Pulayar community. Within the local dialect of North Malabar, the word 'Thondachan' serves as a substitute term for grandfather. The roots of this tradition are anchored in a detailed local legend concerning a heroic figure who underwent a supernatural metamorphosis.

The narrative of the deity begins with his mortal origins. Kari was born to parents named Vallikudichi Virunthi and Maniyan Kanjan. His parents had been brought from Tiruvarkat Kav to work on the agricultural lands belonging to Kunjambu Nair, a jenmi residing at the Chenicherry house in Kunhimangalam. During his early education, Kari studied reading and writing under the guidance of Chempitar Kurikkal. Aspiring to further his martial training, Kari sought to study kalari vidya. However, because he belonged to the Pulayar community, he was initially denied admission to the traditional training grounds.

To bypass this systemic barrier, Kunjambu Nair devised a solution by allowing Kari to use his own name and family name in place of Kari's actual identity. Under this guise, Kari trained extensively across eighteen different kalaris throughout the region. Eventually, he learned the art of impersonation from Chothi Kalari, gaining the magical ability to alter his disguise into various creatures such as a scorpion, a snake, a dog, or a lion. Upon completing his rigorous education, Kari returned to Madai Kalari, where he earned the prestigious position of Kurikal. During this period of his life, he married a young woman named Kunhivellachi.

Kari's exceptional skills eventually drew the attention of regional authorities. The lord of Alladam suffered from severe insanity and summoned Kari on six separate occasions to provide treatment, though Kari was repeatedly prevented from attending. The seventh request arrived via a formal copper inscription, promising that half of the lord's property would be granted if Kari successfully cured him. Setting out for Alladam, Kari overcame numerous trials along the journey using his acquired magical expertise. Upon his arrival, he successfully performed the necessary magical rituals, which cured the lord's mental affliction.

However, wishing to avoid surrendering half of his property as promised, the lord plotted to kill Kari despite his recovery. The lord declared he would only relinquish the property if Kari brought back a tiger, tiger's milk, and tiger hair. Returning home, Kari prepared to retrieve these items by transforming himself into a leopard. Before leaving, he instructed his wife not to panic if he returned in leopard form, telling her to dip a broom in dung water and slap his face. Ascending the mountain, Kari successfully used his magical skills to change his body into a leopard. He returned to Alladam, delivered the demanded tiger elements, and fulfilled the lord's harsh condition.

When Kari arrived back at his own home, however, his wife became terrified upon seeing the leopard and bolted the door shut. Failing to follow his prior instructions, she forced Kari—now trapped in his animal form—to enter through the roof. In the ensuing chaos, he killed his wife, jumped out of the house, and permanently disappeared into the deep forest. Following this tragic event, the lord of Alladam relapsed into his state of insanity. Recognizing that this affliction stemmed from the mistreatment of Kari Kurikal, the local people began worshipping him as Pulimaranja Thondachan, a name signifying the tiger who disappeared.

Beyond ritual worship and the sacred performance of theyyam, the legend of Pulimaranja Thondachan has crossed over into modern regional culture. The myth inspired the literary play Pulijanmam, written by author N Prabhakaran. This theatrical work was subsequently adapted into a Malayalam feature film of the same title, directed by Priyanandanan. Through both traditional religious observance and contemporary artistic expression, the legacy of Pulimaranja Thondachan continues to endure in Kerala.
